title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6604 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

title: October US advance goods trade balance -149.5B vs -133.0B expected
body: Prior was -135.9B That's going leave a dent in GDP forecasts. Elsewhere: Wholesale inventories +0.9% vs +0.8% prior Retail inventories ex autos +0.6% vs +0.7% prior The inventory data should somewhat offset the drag from trade. For background, the advance international trade in goods report is published by the Census Bureau at 8:30 am ET as part of its Advance Economic Indicators release, roughly four weeks after the reference month ends. It's the earliest monthly read on US trade flows and lands alongside advance estimates for wholesale and retail inventories, making it a key input for GDP tracking. The headline is the seasonally adjusted US goods trade deficit, the gap between the value of goods imported and exported. Both sides are broken down into six end-use categories: foods, feeds and beverages; industrial supplies and materials; capital goods; automotive vehicles, parts and engines; consumer goods; and other goods. The figures are in nominal dollars on a Census basis. The advance report covers goods only. Services, where the US runs a surplus in areas such as travel, financial services and intellectual property, are added in the full international trade report from the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Economic Analysis about a week later. That report also revises the advance goods numbers and adds country-level detail. For markets, the main relevance is GDP.

title: Black Friday's Record Spending Trap: Why Good Economic News Isn't Always Good Market News
body: Black Friday could deliver another record-breaking day for US consumer spending, with unprecedented retail sales painting a picture of remarkable consumer resilience. And yet financial markets could still respond negatively. That is not a contradiction. It reflects one of the most important distinctions in trading: the difference between good news and news that is better than expected. Financial markets are forward-looking. By the time Black Friday spending figures arrive, investors have already formed expectations about consumer demand, corporate earnings, inflation and monetary policy. Against the backdrop of a technology-led equity market correction and renewed questions over AI valuations, consumer resilience could offer investors a reason to look elsewhere for earnings growth. But the significance of Black Friday lies less in whether records are broken and more in whether the assumptions underpinning current asset valuations are challenged. title: Connecting the dots: When does the AI selloff become a Fed problem?
body: At what point does Nvidia's falling share price become the Fed's headache? Now, wait a second. That sounds a little silly, doesn't it? But given how much of the US economic growth story is riding on AI these days, I wouldn't laugh off that question so easily. Let's say you have made a decent amount of money from the stock market over the past few years. You're feeling a little richer and perhaps more comfortable about booking that family holiday or even splurging on a new car. But out of nowhere, a good chunk of those gains disappears in just a matter of weeks. Suddenly, that old car doesn't look so bad after all now, does it? Economists call this the wealth effect. And you don't necessarily have to sell your stocks to change your spending habits. Just the notion of feeling poorer can be enough. And while stock market wealth is largely concentrated among the richer households, a prolonged selloff could still take some of the shine off US consumer spending as a whole. This is where the AI boom also puts food on a lot more tables than we might realise. Take for example building a data centre. It isn't just about buying a truckload of Nvidia chips. You need construction workers, electricians, cooling equipment, power supplies and plenty of other things. Just think that there are entire businesses banking on the assumption that the tech giants will keep spending as aggressively as they have been.

title: Germany unemployment rises more than expected in November as labour market struggles persist
body: Germany November unemployment change 9k vs 4k expected Prior 4k Germany November unemployment rate 6.4% vs 6.4% expected Prior 6.4% The number of people out of work in Germany rose by more than expected in November, though the jobless rate is seen holding steady on the month at 6.4%. Overall, the total number of unemployed persons rose to 3.025 million in seasonally adjusted terms. But when looking at the unadjusted total, it fell by 19,000 to 2.936 million in November with the labour office noting that the decline reflected the end of the autumn seasonal pickup. However, I'd put more weight on the seasonally adjusted figures here as they strip out the usual seasonal fluctuations and offer a better indication of the underlying health of the labour market. As for the overall report, the labour office noted that "the trend of recent months is continuing" and that "the slight economic recovery has not led to revival in the labour market in November". If you couple that with the subdued consumer confidence figures yesterday, then you can see why there are still concerns about the sustainability of the recovery. If households become more worried about job security, they're more likely to hold back on spending. That will then give businesses even less incentive to expand and hire. In turn, it also makes life more complicated for the ECB, which is still having to contend with elevated inflation despite pockets of economic weakness across the region.

The added good news is that core annual inflation was also estimated to drop to 2.6% in November, as compared to the 3.1% reading in the month before. That being said, these figures are all still too high for any comfort for the ECB. And that's the troubling part for the central bank as they are dealing with quite an array of inflation backdrops across the region at this stage. But as a whole, policymakers are arguably very much concerned about the risks of potential second-round effects. So, that remains the priority in terms of policy setting. As things stand, they are likely to be able to get away with another rate hike in December. And the market pricing reflects roughly 93% odds of a 25 bps move already. But in looking to next year, the challenge will be how the central bank balances any further tightening measures against slowing economic growth. title: France Q3 GDP revised lower as economic woes deepen
body: France Q3 final GDP -0.2% vs -0.1% q/q prelim Prior 0.0% Ouch. France was already the troubling spot in the euro area and the negative revision to the preliminary GDP estimates only continues to underscore that notion. In volume terms, the French economy contracted by 0.2% in Q3 following some tentative stability in the previous quarter. Domestic demand was pretty much subdued, stagnating on the quarter, while inventory changes contributed to 0.3% to quarterly GDP with net foreign trade being the main drag with a negative contribution of 0.6% on the quarter. Overall, the French economy is seen growing by just 0.1% so far this year and that is hardly encouraging for Europe's second-largest economy. As such, this won't steer the conversation away from stagflationary risks as we head into next year. The only good news is that the latest French inflation numbers for November is at least showing some signs of cooling, affording the ECB some added breathing room in looking to the French economy as a whole. title: France inflation undershoots estimates in November as energy and services price pressures ease

The drop here is even below analyst estimates, with headline annual inflation dropping back below 3%. The monthly reading also shows that French inflation should ease by 0.7% in November, after having risen by 0.4% in October. Looking at the details, energy inflation falling off is a key factor driving that development. Of note, energy prices are seen rising by 19.2% in November compared to the 24.1% increase in October. That being said, core prices are also likely to come off the boil as services inflation cooled as well. Services prices were seen down to 2.3% in November compared to 2.6% in the month before. All in all, the ECB can take some comfort in that as this will reduce stagflationary risks in Europe's second-largest economy. But even then, price pressures are admittedly still on the higher side and policymakers cannot rest on their laurels just yet. For now, all of this still supports the argument that they may perhaps get away with another rate hike. But after, they will have to seriously consider the balance of risks between overtightening monetary policy and the necessity to tame the inflation monster amid potential second-round effects.

title: US reportedly urged Venezuela, Iraq to consider quitting OPEC earlier this year
body: US president Trump has never been much of a fan of OPEC. And as it would seem, he'd quite like a few of its members to feel the same way. In an exclusive report by Reuters today, the US administration is said to have encouraged Venezuela and Iraq to contemplate leaving OPEC earlier this year. Washington reportedly even blocked Venezuela's annual membership payment, while Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman intervened over the summer to persuade the US to back off. Despite such actions, the US State Department has maintained that an OPEC exit was not raised at senior levels with Venezuela and that discussions with Iraq centred on energy infrastructure. Sure, sure. Now, this is all very on brand for Trump given his longstanding disdain for OPEC and the bloc's influence over oil prices. However, there is also arguably a commercial angle here. If Washington wants US oil companies to ramp up production in both countries, why have a third party dictating how much oil they can pump out of the ground? Having said all that, the political realities are a little more complicated though. For Venezuela, which is currently exempt from OPEC production quotas, walking away offers little to no immediate benefit. They would essentially be giving up its seat at the table before their oil industry has even fully recovered. Meanwhile, Iraq's oil ministry has maintained that their position is more in favour of negotiating a bigger production allowance over leaving the bloc altogether.
